claims.text: If a Nigerian company declares a dividend out of profits on which no tax is payable because there are no total profits, the company paying the dividend is charged to tax.
The same applies where total profits are less than the dividend declared, whether or not the recipient is a Nigerian company.

The company is charged at the rate prescribed in section 56 of the Act, as if the dividend were the company's total profits for the year of assessment to which the accounts, out of which the dividend is declared, relate.
This rule does not apply to dividends declared out of retained earnings, to the extent the profits or gains in them have been taxed under the Act.
It also does not apply to dividends declared out of profits or gains that are exempt from income tax by the Act, or to franked investment income as provided in the Act.

It also does not apply to distributions by a real estate investment company to its shareholders from rental income and dividend income received on behalf of those shareholders, whether paid out of profits of the year of declaration or of previous reporting periods.

gaps: The rate in section 56 of the Act is not among the passages, so the rate cannot be stated.
The meaning of franked investment income is not given in the passages.
Any tax a recipient or the payer must deduct at source on the dividend under section 51 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 is not set out in the passages.

claims.text: A non-resident person who makes taxable supplies to Nigeria must register for tax and include VAT on its invoice for all taxable supplies.

Where a non-resident makes taxable supplies from outside Nigeria to persons in Nigeria, the taxable person in Nigeria to whom the supply is made must withhold the VAT due on the supply and remit it to the Service.
The Service may, by notice, appoint any person, including a non-resident supplier, to collect the VAT and remit it to the Service.

If such an appointed person has made the supply to a taxable person in Nigeria, the Nigerian taxable person has no obligation to withhold the VAT, unless the appointed person has failed to collect it.
A non-resident supplier may appoint a representative to handle its VAT compliance.
The Service may direct a taxable person who is issued an invoice on which VAT is not included to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service.

VAT that is collected, withheld or self-accounted under section 155 must be remitted on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction, or as the Service prescribes.

The remittance must come with a schedule showing the name, Tax ID and address of the contractor or supplier, invoice number, gross amount of invoice, amount of the VAT and the month to which the return relates.
A person who must collect VAT must keep proper records and make returns and remittances, and the compliance rules apply to that person as though it were the taxable person.
A foreign company is defined as a company other than a Nigerian company, and in the Nigeria Tax Act it also includes a non-resident company.

gaps: Whether your software supply is a taxable supply is not covered by these passages.
Whether the foreign company has been appointed by the Service under section 151(3) is not stated, so which party accounts depends on that fact.
Section 155 and section 158 are marked as disputed, meaning another official text reads differently somewhere in them; this answer follows the text as printed.
Any guidelines or notices issued by the Service are not among the passages.

claims.text: In the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, a small company is one with gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less per annum and total fixed assets not exceeding ₦250,000,000.
The definition says any business providing professional services shall not be classified as a small company.
So low turnover alone is not enough under that definition if the business provides professional services.

The Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 has a similar definition of small business, with gross turnover of ₦100,000,000 or less and total fixed assets less than ₦250,000,000. It also excludes any business providing professional services.
A small company is taxed at 0%, and any other company at 30 per cent from the commencement of the Act.
A small company's tax return may contain a statement of accounts attested to by the taxpayer instead of audited financial statements.

gaps: The passages do not say what counts as professional services, so they do not settle whether a consulting firm is one.
The passages do not say whether consulting is a professional service, so the answer depends on that point.
The passages show the two Acts use different figures for small company and small business; the passages do not explain how they relate.

claims.text: Table I lists Motor Vehicle Expenditure under Class 3, which has a rate of 25%.

Capital allowance is made at the rate specified in Table I for each year of assessment in the basis period for which the asset was used for the purposes of the trade or business, where the expenditure was incurred wholly and exclusively for that trade or business.
The allowance is made only if, at the end of the basis period, the company owns the asset and used it for the purposes of its trade or business.
If the basis period is less than one year, the allowance for that year is granted proportionately.
An allowance is not made unless it is claimed for that year, or the relevant tax authority thinks it would be just to the taxpayer and reasonable to make it.

The law says 1% of the qualifying capital expenditure is recorded in the capital allowance computation schedule for statistical purposes. This is a notional amount and does not increase or reduce the capital allowance claimable.

gaps: The passages do not define whether a particular company car falls within Motor Vehicle Expenditure, nor how many years the allowance runs.
The actual allowance amount for any year would need a calculation on the car's cost and residue, which is not done here.

claims.text: If the relevant tax authority finds or thinks that a taxable person was not assessed, or was assessed at too little, it may assess the right amount or the additional amount within six years of the assessment.
The six-year limit does not stop the tax authority from continuing a tax audit and raising an additional assessment, if the audit began before the six years ended.

Where there is a deliberate misstatement connected with any tax under the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025 or any other tax law, the tax authority may assess at any time, and as often as needed, to make good the loss of tax caused by the misstatement.
All relevant facts are considered when working out the extra tax, even if they were not known when an earlier assessment for the same year was made.

Once an assessment is final and conclusive, the tax authority can still make an assessment or additional assessment for that year, as long as it does not re-open an issue on the same facts that was already settled by agreement or on appeal.

gaps: The passages print the period as running from "the assessment", not from the filing of the return. Which date applies to your case depends on when the assessment was made.

questions.question: My company made ₦120 million profit this year. How much company income tax will it pay?

claims.text: Company income tax is charged on the total profits of every company for each year of assessment.
A small company is taxed at 0%.
Any other company is taxed at 30 per cent from the commencement of the Act.
Total profits are the total assessable profits from all sources, including chargeable gains, less any loss and less capital allowance.

A company must include dividend income in its profits, gross of any tax paid or deducted at source. Dividends a Nigerian company receives by way of shares of the paying company are not included in its profits chargeable to tax.

If a company's effective tax rate for a year is less than 15%, it must recompute and pay additional tax to bring the rate to 15%. This applies to a constituent entity of an MNE group, and to any other company with aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment.

gaps: The passages do not say whether your company is a small company, so the applicable rate (0% or 30 per cent) cannot be determined. The definition of a small company is not in the passages.
The ₦120 million is described as profit, not total profits. Total profits depend on adjustments such as losses and capital allowances, and the passages do not give your figures.
Applying the rate to the profit figure is a calculation, which is not done here.
Whether the 15% effective tax rate rule applies depends on your company's turnover or group status, which is not stated.

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4): The National Assembly text requires companies in the priority sector to obtain a certificate of acceptance from the Industrial Inspectorate Department for qualifying capital expenditure; the gazette has no such condition. (DR-039)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8: Cross-reference: the gazette cites section 51 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, the National Assembly text section 50. (DR-007, DR-008)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The minimum tax is measured differently. Gazette: covered tax paid divided by profits, where profits are net profit before tax less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost. National Assembly: covered taxes (companies income tax, petroleum profit tax, hydrocarbon tax, development levy, priority sector tax credit) as a percentage of net income, which excludes franked investment income and unrealised gains or losses. (DR-051)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette applies the 15% minimum to every constituent entity of an MNE group; the National Assembly text only where the group's turnover is at least 750 million (printed with a pound sign) or its equivalent. (DR-052)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The 15% minimum effective tax rate applies from an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 in the gazette and ₦50,000,000,000 in the National Assembly text. (DR-053)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The National Assembly text exempts approved free-zone enterprises (except for sales into the customs territory and MNE entities) and lets the Service set a higher turnover threshold by regulation; the gazette has neither and measures turnover in the relevant year of assessment rather than the financial year. (DR-054)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette numbers the subsections (1), (2) and (4), with no (3); the labels are kept as printed. The National Assembly text has (1) to (4). (DR-055)

questions.question: Under section 191 of the Nigeria Tax Act, where do objections and appeals go?

claims.text: Section 191 lets a relevant tax authority disregard a disposition or transaction it considers artificial or fictitious, or direct adjustments to tax liability, and issue an assessment or additional assessment.
The provisions on objections and appeals under Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025 apply to a direction made under section 191.

The passages supplied from the Administration Act are in Chapter Two, section 41, not Chapter Four. Under that section, an objection goes to the relevant tax authority as a written notice, delivered in person, by courier service or by electronic means.
The objection is valid only if it is delivered within 30 days from the date of service of the disputed notice of assessment and contains the grounds of objection listed in section 41(2)(b).
The relevant tax authority may extend that time for satisfactory and good cause shown.
The relevant tax authority must respond to the objection notice within 90 days, otherwise the objection of the taxpayer is upheld.
If the authority considers the objection invalid, or the two sides do not agree on the amount of tax, the taxpayer may exercise the right of appeal.
A party unhappy with the High Court's decision may appeal to the Court of Appeal, and an appeal from the Court of Appeal goes to the Supreme Court.

gaps: Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025, which section 191(2) refers to, is not among the passages.
The passages do not say which body first hears an appeal before the High Court, so the route from the taxpayer's right of appeal to the High Court is not stated.
